PRODUCT APPROACH

How I approach product work.

I do not have a professional Product Manager title yet. What I do have is repeated practice turning customer and workflow problems into structured decisions, scoped solutions, shipped work, and learning loops.

01

Understand the problem

Look for repeated friction, user context, constraints, and the job that actually needs to get done.

02

Define the product bet

Turn the problem into a clear hypothesis about what should change and why it could create value.

03

Scope the MVP

Protect the core loop, make tradeoffs explicit, and separate must-have value from future depth.

04

Ship and validate

Get the product into real use, capture failure points, and fix what blocks value.

05

Learn and decide

Use behavior, feedback, defects, and outcomes to decide what should change next.

02 • MileStory

The user problem was personal. The product thinking had to be disciplined.

INDEPENDENT PRODUCT • PUBLICLY LAUNCHED

A running app built around the story behind the race.

Most running products are great at recording activities. What they miss is the larger journey. MileStory started with that gap and became a real 0→1 product exercise in problem framing, scope, prioritization, release, post-launch QA, and iteration. It is publicly available on both the App Store and Google Play.

Why it matters

This is the clearest proof that I can take a problem from observation to product logic, then stay close enough to execution to learn from what breaks.

Problem

Runners track workouts, but lose the story.

Training for a race is a multi-week narrative. Existing products often break that experience into isolated activities.

Product Bet

Make the Journey the core object.

Runs, milestones, photos, and updates become chapters inside a larger race goal instead of disconnected posts.

MVP

Ship the loop before shipping every feature.

Journey creation, race setup, countdowns, feed, Explore, profiles, engagement, milestones, and Strava-connected progress.

Tradeoff

Protect the core loop first.

Broader social depth came later. The first priority was making the journey itself worth returning to.

Testing

Use release friction as product evidence.

TestFlight, beta feedback, navigation issues, onboarding fixes, and data-state problems all fed the next iteration.

Learning

Social features cannot rescue a weak core product loop.

The product has to create individual value before community features can amplify it.

AFTER LAUNCH

Shipping was the start of the learning loop.

I am not presenting early usage as scale. I am using it as proof that the product is live, has real users, and is already generating concrete post-launch learning.

iOS + AndroidPublicly launched
13iOS lifetime downloads
4Active users in the last 30 days via Supabase
3–4Steady active Android devices
QA SIGNAL

Password visibility was missing.

PrimeTestLab flagged the sign-in friction during structured device testing.

Decision → Added a password-visibility toggle.
LAYOUT ISSUE

System UI obscured content on some devices.

SafeAreaView was imported from the wrong package across seven screens, creating layout issues across devices.

Decision → Corrected the implementation across affected screens.
INPUT + KEYBOARD ISSUE

Keyboard behavior was inconsistent across devices.

KeyboardAvoidingView behavior was undefined across the same seven screens, creating inconsistent keyboard handling.

Decision → Corrected the keyboard-avoidance behavior across the affected screens.
FOLLOW-ON LEARNING

A cross-device fix exposed an additional iOS layout bug.

A height rule on an auto-sizing parent caused an additional layout issue on iOS.

Decision → Reworked positioning to use top: 0 and bottom: 0.
WHAT THIS PROVES

The useful signal is not the size of the user base yet. It is that I can ship a real product, put it in front of users and testers, identify where the experience breaks, trace issues to implementation decisions, and iterate after launch.

03 • BRQ

Productizing a problem that kept showing up before kickoff.

Business Requirements Questionnaire

Discovery should start with clarity.

Across implementation work, the same categories of context repeatedly had to be gathered before teams could move cleanly into delivery. I reframed that recurring operational pain as a product opportunity: make intake easier for the customer and more useful for the Implementation team.

Problem

Requirements, stakeholders, timelines, and readiness details arrive inconsistently.

My role

Problem framing, workflow design, interface concept, and prototype development.

What I built

Guided questions, institution personalization, save-and-return behavior, and exportable handoff output.

Learning

Reducing ambiguity can improve both customer experience and operational efficiency.

Status

Used internally and adopted across the Implementation team.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE SUCCESS
Completion rateAre users finishing the intake?
Pre-kickoff readinessHow much required context is available before kickoff?
Clarification loadDoes post-kickoff back-and-forth decrease?
Time to usable requirementsDoes the workflow reduce manual information gathering?
Save + return behaviorCan users complete longer intake without starting over?
04 • Nelnet Campus Commerce

Enterprise delivery taught me where product friction actually shows up.

I do not own the Nelnet product roadmap. My current Implementation Project Manager role puts me directly inside the customer journey for higher education payment products, where I manage 16–18 concurrent implementations and maintain 98% on-time delivery while seeing recurring friction across onboarding, integrations, testing, launch preparation, and adoption.

Signal

Institutions repeatedly surface needs around setup, integrations, permissions, testing, communication, and launch readiness.

My lens

I translate customer friction into clearer requirements, stronger workflows, handoff improvements, and product or process opportunities.

Product value

Direct implementation exposure helps distinguish one-off requests from repeatable problems worth solving at the product level.

Outcome

A stronger understanding of the adoption journey from customer intent through technical integration, testing, and real-world use.
